tone_statements.citation: Versloot, Arjen P. 2008. Mechanisms of Language Change: Vowel Reduction in 15th Century West Frisian. PhD dissertation, Rijksuniversiteit Groningen (promotor G.J. de Haan). LOT Dissertation Series 195. Utrecht: LOT. 382 pp. ISBN 978-90-78328-69-8.
tone_statements.quote: In other West Germanic languages, intensity stress and pitch accent were aligned on the same syllable: The stressed root. 15th century West Frisian developed the possibility of having those two stress markers on different syllables, independent of the quality of the second syllable. Minimal pairs developed, such as wesen with Accent II in the gerund but with Accent I in the past participle. The tone contour became an independent marker of semantic and morphological functions. [...] [p. 295:] In modern language, the pitch accent is aligned with the intensity stress at the beginning of the stressed syllable.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 4.7 'The phonologisation of tone contours', p. 252; sec. 4.9 p. 256 ('At the end of the period, early-Modern Frisian was a language with tonal contrasts comparable with Scandinavian languages'); sec. 6.1 p. 295 ('M inimal' normalised in the quote)
tone_statements.summary: Reconstructed for 15th-century West Frisian: a two-way word tone-contour (tonal accent) opposition, Accent I vs Accent II, arising from a delayed pitch peak after unstressed /a/, lexicalised by lemma/morphological category alongside root-initial intensity stress; in Modern West Frisian pitch accent coincides with stress (no tonal contrast).

sources.note: Abstract (Crossref) does not mention tone: argues that Riustring Vowel Balance (i/u after light stems, e/o after heavy and polysyllabic stems) is a prosodically driven reduction process captured by a foot-based analysis, with caveats on trimoraic vowel balance in disyllables and the i~e contrast as a marker of stem size.
